questions.question: Distinguish economic development from economic growth, explain how the HDI measures development, and state what South Africa's income-versus-HDI gap reveals.
questions.expected_answer: Growth is a quantity statement — real GDP rose; development is a quality statement — lives improved through better health, education and falling poverty. The HDI combines three dimensions: income per capita, life expectancy and education (years of schooling), scoring countries between 0 and 1. South Africa ranks upper-middle by income but noticeably lower on the HDI because life expectancy and learning outcomes lag behind what our production predicts — we are richer than we are healthy or educated, i.e. growth has outrun development.

questions.question: Name the six common characteristics of developing countries and show, for any two, how South Africa 'fits with a twist'.
questions.expected_answer: Low standard of living; low productivity; high population growth and dependency burdens; high unemployment/underemployment; dependence on the primary sector and raw exports; deficient infrastructure and incomplete markets. Twists: on living standards, SA's average income is upper-middle but extreme inequality leaves millions in absolute poverty beneath the average — a distribution problem more than an average problem; on unemployment SA is extreme rather than typical (over 30% official, over 40% expanded); on primary dependence, production is service-dominated yet exports still lean on minerals, keeping the old vulnerability in the trade accounts.

questions.question: Explain what Indigenous Knowledge Systems contribute to development, and use the hoodia and rooibos cases to show why legal protection matters.
questions.expected_answer: IKS — knowledge, practices and institutions built over generations — contributes working development infrastructure: stokvels and burial societies mobilise tens of billions in savings and insurance among people banks ignored; drought-resistant crops like sorghum and intercropping suit a drying climate; traditional medicine reaches most South Africans; customary institutions manage communal resources. Development that ignores trusted institutions tends to fail, so policy should build on them. Protection: the San's hoodia knowledge was patented without consent or payment — biopiracy — and only years of struggle produced a benefit-sharing agreement; rooibos communities won recognition and now earn a share. Indigenous knowledge is an asset, and law must ensure its holders consent and benefit.
